text:
Training many different machine learning models and averaging their predictions can improve performance [P3_p1_c02]. However, using a whole ensemble of models is cumbersome and computationally expensive, making it hard to deploy to many users, especially when the individual models are large neural networks [P3_p1_c02]. 

Training sets can also be very large, leading to excessive computation during training even when parallelized [P3_p5_c04]. Meanwhile, deploying systems to many users has strict requirements on speed and computational resources [P3_p1_c03]. 

The paper solves this by using a technique called distillation to transfer the knowledge from a large ensemble of models into a single, smaller model [P3_p1_c02][P3_p1_c03]. This approach frees knowledge from a specific model instance by viewing it more abstractly [P3_p1_c04]. It also introduces a new type of ensemble made of full models and specialist models that learn to separate fine-grained classes [P3_p1_c02]. These specialist models can be trained rapidly and in parallel [P3_p1_c02].

Regarding results, the paper shows surprising outcomes on the MNIST dataset and significantly improves the acoustic model of a heavily used commercial system by distilling an ensemble into a single model [P3_p1_c02]. The single model works significantly better than a same-sized model learned directly from the same training data [P3_p4_c03]. Furthermore, using soft targets allows a baseline speech model to recover almost all information in the full training set using only 3 percent of the data, which is about 20M examples, avoiding severe overfitting [P3_p7_c03]. The sources do not state limitations beyond noting that specialist models tend to overfit easily unless prevented [P3_p5_c04].
